sections.label: What a skill is
sections.h2: A prompt you never have to write again.
body: A skill is a file that tells the AI how to do one job: the purpose, the steps in order, the rules, the output format, and one or two examples of it done right. In Claude Code these live in a folder and load when you name them. In other tools they are saved prompts or custom instructions. Same idea.
The difference between a prompt and a skill is repetition. A prompt is what you type once. A skill is what you would otherwise type every week.
If you have a note somewhere titled 'the prompt that works for X,' that note is a skill waiting to be filed.

sections.label: When you need one
sections.h2: Three signs you need a skill.
body: You keep pasting the same setup paragraph before the real request.
The AI does the job well on the third try and badly on the first, every time.
Two people on your team get different results from the same request.
Each of those is the same problem: the knowledge of how to do the job lives in a person's head or a chat history instead of in a file the AI can read.

sections.label: What is inside
body: One sentence. What the job is and when to use this skill.
What the AI needs from you before it starts. A transcript, a name, a number. If it is missing, the skill says to ask.
The job in order. Short, numbered, no adjectives.
What it must never do. This is where your judgment lives. Do not invent quotes. Do not promise results. Keep it under 200 words.
Exactly what the output looks like, and one real example of it done right.

# Sales debrief skill

Purpose: turn my notes from one customer conversation into a coaching plan.
Inputs: the notes or transcript, names removed.
Steps: 1) state the customer's problem in their words ... 5) give one follow-up question.
Rules: use only what is in the notes. Never invent a motive.
Format: five numbered sections, under 250 words.
Example: [paste one good output]

sections.label: Prompting with skills
sections.h2: The prompt shrinks to one line.
body: Before: three paragraphs of setup, then the request. After: 'Run the sales debrief skill on these notes.' The AI loads the file, follows the steps, applies the rules, returns the format. If it drifts, you fix the skill file once, not the prompt every time.
Your prompts got shorter and your results got more consistent in the same week. That is the whole point.

pr: Turn a repeated prompt into a skill.
Paste a prompt you keep rewriting. The AI restructures it into the five parts.
prompt: Here is a prompt I keep rewriting: [paste it] Turn it into a skill file with exactly five parts: Purpose (one sentence), Inputs (what I must provide, and what to ask for if missing), Steps (numbered, short, no adjectives), Rules (what you must never do, including: never invent facts, never promise results), Format (what the output looks like, with a word limit). 1. Keep the whole file under 250 words. 2. Where my prompt was vague, write the rule you think I meant and mark it [confirm]. 3. Finish with the one-line prompt I will type from now on to run it.
